chapter_title: Basic Logic Gates: And, Or, Not, Xor, and Their Multi-bit Versions

screens.title: Basic Logic Gates and Their Multi‑bit Versions
screens.subtitle: From single Nand primitives to Not16, And16, Or16, Xor16 and Or8Way zero detection

narration.text: In this lesson we will deepen your practical understanding of the gates that form every digital computer: Not, And, Or, and Xor — and how to scale them from single bits to 16‑bit buses. You will see how each 1‑bit gate is implemented using the single available primitive, Nand, and how the simple idea of replication turns 1‑bit logic into a 16‑bit workhorse such as And16. We will also explore the multi‑way Or gate, Or8Way, built as a tree of two‑input Or gates and why it is useful for detecting whether a whole word is zero. Along the way you will learn how to think about buses as arrays of parallel operations, how to verify these chips using representative test vectors, and how gate counts reflect parallelism and area cost. A short, concrete example you will work through is the Not16 chip: by applying Not to each bit in parallel you invert an entire 16‑bit word in a single logical step. Finally, we will practice composing Or8Way with a final Or and a Not to implement zero detection for a 16‑bit value. Keep this practical question in mind as we go: how does parallel replication change performance and hardware cost compared to reusing a single gate sequentially?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A handful of 1‑bit gates built from Nand, replicated across all bits of a bus, becomes the multi‑bit primitives that the ALU and CPU use to process words in parallel.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Introduction
Basic Logic Gates and Their Multi‑bit Versions
How to build 1‑bit gates from Nand, replicate them for buses, and use Or8Way for zero detection.
What you'll understand

How Not, And, Or, and Xor come from Nand; how to implement Not16/And16/Or16/Xor16 by replication; how Or8Way is composed as a tree; and how to verify these chips with test scripts.

Why it matters

Multi‑bit gates let hardware operate on full words in parallel. These primitives are reused throughout the ALU, registers, and memory systems you will build next.

Explore Key Topics
Gate from Nand
Every 1‑bit gate can be expressed with Nand. This keeps the design minimal and instructive.
Bus replication
Replicate a 1‑bit gate 16 times to operate on 16‑bit words in parallel.
Or8Way & Zero detect
Use a tree of Ors to detect any high bit in a group and compose for zero detection.
Visual concept
Imagine two 16‑bit trains passing through 16 paired gates, producing a 16‑car output train.
// Example 1‑bit identities
// Not(x)  = Nand(x, x)
// And(x,y)= Not(Nand(x,y))
// Or(x,y) = Nand(Not(x), Not(y))
// Xor(x,y)= (x && !y) || (!x && y)
Key Takeaway

Build complex word operations by composing simple, tested 1‑bit gates across a bus. The hardware cost scales linearly with the number of bits because each bit is processed independently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do by the end of this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement the four basic logic gates using only the Nand primitive, and then scale those gates to operate on 16‑bit buses. You will build Not16, And16, Or16, and Xor16 by systematically replicating the corresponding 1‑bit construction across a sixteen‑line bus, and you will construct Or8Way using a balanced tree of two‑input Or gates. You will also learn to use Or8Way in a short circuit to detect whether a 16‑bit word is zero by combining the outputs of two Or8Way blocks and a final Not. Finally, you will verify each HDL implementation with the Hardware Simulator and representative test vectors such as all zeros, all ones, and alternating patterns. These skills matter because they show how low‑level primitives compose into the multi‑bit operations used throughout the ALU and memory systems. In practice this helps you reason about parallelism, gate count, and testing choices when designing hardware.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Reasoning
screens.subtitle: Skills, testing, and hardware reasoning you will practice

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on practical reasoning: you will write HDL that instantiates 16 copies of a 1‑bit gate to make a 16‑bit chip, and you will learn to reason about gate counts and parallel cost. You will practice preparing test scripts with representative values such as all zeros, all ones, and alternating patterns like the hex patterns suggested in the text; these help catch wiring mistakes and bit-order errors. You will also learn the standard circuit for zero detection: split a 16‑bit word into two 8‑bit halves, apply Or8Way to each half, then combine and invert appropriately to produce an IsZero signal. Finally, you will reflect on why hardware designers prefer fixed-width buses: parallelism gives single‑cycle word operations at the cost of linear area. These exercises train both HDL syntax and engineering judgment about test selection and tradeoffs in area versus latency.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Practice
Test vectors to try

  • All ones (0xFFFF) — ensures gates react to full ones across the bus.

screens.title: 1‑Bit Gate Definitions: Not, And, Or, Xor
screens.subtitle: Formal identities and intuitive meanings

narration.text: Let's start with a clear definition for each 1‑bit gate and its intuitive role. Not simply flips a single input bit: when input is one, the output is zero and vice versa. In this course Not is implemented directly as Nand(x,x), which shows how inversion can come from the Nand primitive. And outputs one only when both inputs are one; you can implement it by inverting the Nand result, or conceptually think of it as a single gate that requires both signals to be present. Or outputs one when at least one input is one: in our construction it uses Nand and two Not operations to realize logical disjunction. Xor is the exclusive-or: it outputs one only when exactly one input is one. Another way to express Xor is the disjunction of two conjunctions: (x and not y) or (not x and y). A concrete example ties these together: if x=1 and y=0, Not(x) = 0, And(x,y) = 0, Or(x,y) = 1, and Xor(x,y) = 1. A common misconception is to think Xor is just 'not equal' on bits; that is true for 1‑bit inputs but it requires care when extending to multi‑bit words because you must apply Xor per bit. Takeaway: each gate has a precise boolean identity and a role in composing higher‑level arithmetic and comparison circuits. Try the simple example numbers in the simulator to confirm you understand each truth case.

keyIdea.title: Definition focus
keyIdea.text: Understand the exact logical truth each 1‑bit gate implements, because these identities drive correct HDL implementations and replication.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › 1‑Bit Gates
Not

Definition: output is the logical complement of input. Identity used: Not(x) = Nand(x, x).

Concrete example: if input = 1, Not = 0. If input = 0, Not = 1.
And

Definition: output is 1 only if both inputs are 1. Implemented as Not(Nand(x,y)).

Common misconception: And is not the same as multiplication on multi‑bit words unless you apply it bitwise.
Or and Xor

Or returns 1 if at least one input is 1; Or(x,y) = Nand(Not(x), Not(y)). Xor returns 1 when inputs differ: Xor(x,y) = (x && !y) || (!x && y).

Concrete check: x=1,y=0 gives Or=1 and Xor=1; x=1,y=1 gives Or=1 but Xor=0.
Truth examples and quick table
Inputs: x=1,y=0
Results: Not(x)=0, And=0, Or=1, Xor=1
Inputs: x=1,y=1
Results: Not(x)=0, And=1, Or=1, Xor=0
Common mistake

Treating Xor as simply an adder without carry. Xor is bitwise difference but it does not propagate carry bits; addition requires separate carry logic.

screens.title: Implementing 1‑bit Gates Using Nand
screens.subtitle: Concrete HDL identities and small code examples

narration.text: Now we will look at the exact HDL identities used to express Not, And, Or, and Xor from the single primitive Nand. These are not theoretical exercises only: they are the actual lines you will write in HDL. For example, Not is simply Nand(input, input); that single instantiation flips the bit. And can be written by first computing Nand(x,y) and then applying Not to that value, which in HDL becomes a second Nand. Or uses De Morgan's law: compute Not(x) and Not(y) and then Nand those results together. Xor is a slightly longer expression: it combines two And-like terms with an Or; implemented in HDL by wiring Not and And instances into the Or structure. A concrete HDL snippet helps internalize the wiring: the textbook shows how And16 is implemented by listing 16 And parts, but the same style applies for 1‑bit wiring. A common mistake is to try to share intermediate Nand outputs across bits; remember that in a 1‑bit gate the intermediate signals are local. After you write these small HDL fragments, run the 1‑bit tests to confirm every truth table entry is correct before replicating the gate for a bus. This disciplined approach prevents cascading wiring errors later.

keyIdea.title: From identity to HDL
keyIdea.text: Each logical identity corresponds directly to one or more HDL PARTS lines; test the 1‑bit gates thoroughly before replication.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › HDL Walkthrough
HDL examples (1‑bit)
CHIP Not {
  IN in;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Nand(a=in, b=in, out=out);
}

CHIP And {
  IN a, b;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Nand(a=a, b=b, out=tmp);
  Nand(a=tmp, b=tmp, out=out); // Not(tmp)
}

CHIP Or {
  IN a, b;
  OUT out;

  PARTS:
  Nand(a=a, b=a, out=na);
  Nand(a=b, b=b, out=nb);
  Nand(a=na, b=nb, out=out);
}
Example

Writing Not as a single Nand shows why Nand is a complete primitive: every other gate is composed from it.

Common mistake

Confusing temporary signals across gates. Keep intermediate nets local and test 1‑bit behavior first to avoid scaling errors.

narration.text: And16 is the canonical example of gate replication. Conceptually And16 takes two 16‑bit inputs and produces a 16‑bit output in which each bit is the conjunction of the corresponding input bits. The implementation is mechanical: instantiate And sixteen times, mapping a[0] with b[0] to out[0], and so on through a[15] and b[15]. The supplied HDL pattern shows the repeated PARTS lines. This repetition enforces independence between bits: there is no sharing or carry between the And instances, which is precisely why the hardware cost scales linearly. A concrete HDL fragment clarifies the pattern and the exact wiring you will type into the file. When you run tests, check specific single-bit cases and representative vectors such as 0xFFFF and 0x0000 to ensure every instantiation works. A common misconception is thinking you can reduce gate count by sharing Nand outputs across bits; you cannot, because each bit path must be driven independently. The takeaway is that replication gives single‑cycle parallelism with linear area growth — a tradeoff you will see again in the ALU. Building And16 by Replication means and16 is implemented by 16 independent and instances wired bitwise, illustrating parallelism and linear gate scaling.. In practical terms, pattern: instantiate 16 independent and gates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Replication pattern
keyIdea.text: And16 is implemented by 16 independent And instances wired bitwise, illustrating parallelism and linear gate scaling.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › And16
And16 HDL pattern
CHIP And16 {
  IN a[16], b[16];
  OUT out[16];

  PARTS:
  And(a=a[0], b=b[0], out=out[0]);
  And(a=a[1], b=b[1], out=out[1]);
  // ... repeat through index 15
  And(a=a[15], b=b[15], out=out[15]);
}
This pattern is intentionally repetitive. Each And instance is independent, which keeps timing identical to a single And but multiplies area by sixteen.
Check example

Test with a=0xFFFF, b=0x0001; out should mirror b where only the least significant bit passes the And.

Misconception

Avoid attempts to multiplex a single And over 16 cycles to 'save gates' — that changes latency and violates the parallel model expected by later modules.

narration.text: Not16 applies the inversion operation independently to each of sixteen lines. The HDL mirrors the 1‑bit Not: for each index i you instantiate Not(in=in[i], out=out[i]). This is a clear example of the bus abstraction: the chip has a single 16‑bit input and a single 16‑bit output, but internally it is just sixteen Not gates wired in parallel. A concrete use case is bitwise complement: given a 16‑bit word you can flip every bit in one logical cycle. Students sometimes confuse bitwise inversion with arithmetic negation. They are not the same: bitwise Not flips every bit in place, while arithmetic two's‑complement negation also requires adding one and handling carries. In practice, Not16 is used within larger constructions where bitwise complement is required, for example when implementing Xor16 or subtraction primitives. Always test Not16 with all zeros and all ones: Not16(0x0000) should produce 0xFFFF and Not16(0xFFFF) should produce 0x0000. This simple chip is an important building block because it behaves predictably and composes cleanly with other multi‑bit gates. Not16 and Bitwise Inversion means not16 inverts each bit independently; it is structurally sixteen not gates and is distinct from arithmetic negation.. In practical terms, applying not across a 16‑line bus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Not16 behavior
keyIdea.text: Not16 inverts each bit independently; it is structurally sixteen Not gates and is distinct from arithmetic negation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Not16
Not16 HDL
CHIP Not16 {
  IN in[16];
  OUT out[16];

  PARTS:
  Not(in=in[0], out=out[0]);
  Not(in=in[1], out=out[1]);
  // ... repeat through index 15
  Not(in=in[15], out=out[15]);
}
Example

Not16(0x0000) = 0xFFFF; Not16(0xAAAA) = 0x5555. Use these to sanity‑check wiring and bit ordering.

Misconception

Do not confuse bitwise inversion with arithmetic two's complement negation; they are different operations and implemented differently.

screens.title: Constructing Or16 and Xor16
screens.subtitle: Replicating Or and Xor across sixteen bits

narration.text: Or16 and Xor16 follow the same replication strategy as And16 and Not16: instantiate the corresponding 1‑bit gate sixteen times, wiring each pair of input bits to the matching output bit. For Or16 use Or(a=a[i], b=b[i], out=out[i]) for i from 0 to 15. For Xor16, instantiate Xor similarly. A concrete example: to compute Xor16 for two 16‑bit words representing two binary numbers, you get a 16‑bit result where each bit is one when the inputs differ at that bit position. This bitwise approach is useful for parity checks or masks. When implementing Xor16, remember the 1‑bit Xor formula uses Not and And or can be realized directly by combining gates; however the HDL for Xor16 merely repeats the Xor part. A common source of bugs is bit-order mismatch: ensure your indexing convention is consistent across inputs and tests. To validate, use representative patterns: 0xAAAA XOR 0x5555 should yield 0xFFFF, and 0xFFFF XOR 0xFFFF should yield 0x0000. The lesson is that multi‑bit logical functions are simply parallelized 1‑bit functions, and careful testing of representative vectors quickly reveals index or wiring problems. Constructing Or16 and Xor16 means or16 and xor16 are direct, independent replications of 1‑bit or and xor across all 16 bit positions; verify with representative patterns to catch ordering bugs.. In practical terms, replicating or and xor across sixteen bits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parallelization
keyIdea.text: Or16 and Xor16 are direct, independent replications of 1‑bit Or and Xor across all 16 bit positions; verify with representative patterns to catch ordering bugs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Or16 & Xor16
Replicate Or and Xor
Pattern for Or16 and Xor16 is identical to And16: repeat the 1‑bit gate across indices 0..15. Use representative test vectors to confirm correctness.
// Example test expectations
// Or16(0xAAAA, 0x5555) => 0xFFFF
// Xor16(0xFFFF, 0xFFFF) => 0x0000
Check

If your Xor16 returns 0xFFFF for 0xAAAA ^ 0x5555, indexing is likely correct. If not, inspect bit wiring and test vectors.

Pitfall

Confusing endianness: ensure tests and HDL use the same bit numbering so bit 0 corresponds to the expected least significant position.

screens.title: Or8Way: Building a Multi‑way Or Tree
screens.subtitle: Balanced tree of Or gates for any-high detection

narration.text: Or8Way is a design pattern that reduces eight inputs into a single bit indicating whether any input is high. The approach is to compose two‑input Or gates in a balanced tree: first pair the inputs into four Ors, then pair those results into two Ors, and finally Or the two results. Written compactly, Or8Way(a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h) = Or(Or(Or(a,b), Or(c,d)), Or(Or(e,f), Or(g,h))). This tree structure minimizes gate depth and keeps the number of levels small. A practical example is checking whether any bit in an 8‑bit group is 1; Or8Way returns 1 when at least one is set. Use Or8Way in zero detection by applying it to each 8‑bit half of a 16‑bit word: if both halves produce 0 then the entire word is zero. A common misconception is to try a linear chain of Ors; that increases latency and is unnecessary here. Balanced trees are preferred for predictable depth. When coding Or8Way in HDL, list the Or parts in the same tree order and test with single‑bit inputs set to validate each subtree. The final insight: tree composition trades more gates for reduced logical depth, improving single‑cycle response for parallel checks.

keyIdea.title: Or8Way tree
keyIdea.text: Or8Way reduces eight inputs with a balanced tree of two‑input Or gates, giving a compact, low‑depth detector of any high bit.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Or8Way
Or8Way composition
Use a balanced tree of Or gates. This minimizes levels of logic and keeps the detector fast.
// Expression form:
// Or8Way(a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h) = Or(Or(Or(a,b), Or(c,d)), Or(Or(e,f), Or(g,h)))

// HDL style: instantiate intermediate Or parts and combine.
Concrete test

Set input g high and all others low; Or8Way should return 1, verifying that the subtree containing g is wired correctly.

Pitfall

A linear chain of Ors increases depth unnecessarily; prefer balanced pairing for minimal levels.

screens.title: Zero Detection for a 16‑bit Word
screens.subtitle: Combining Or8Way and Not to test whether a word is zero

narration.text: Zero detection is a simple but essential task: determine if all 16 bits of a word are zero. The recommended circuit uses two Or8Way blocks and a final Not. Split the 16‑bit input into a high half and a low half. Apply Or8Way to each half; each Or8Way returns 1 if any bit in its half is high. If both halves return zero, the whole word is zero. To produce a conventional IsZero signal that is 1 when the word is zero, invert the Or of the two Or8Way outputs: IsZero = Not(Or(Or8Way(high), Or8Way(low))). This circuit is efficient because it reuses the balanced Or8Way structure and a single final Or plus Not, rather than constructing a monolithic 16‑way Or. A concrete example: input 0x0000 gives Or8Way(high)=0 and Or8Way(low)=0, so Or = 0 and Not = 1, indicating zero. A typical misconception is trying to check each bit individually in HDL scripting; using the Or8Way halves composes cleanly and keeps the HDL readable. This pattern is used in the ALU to detect zero flags cheaply and predictably. Zero Detection for a 16‑bit Word means split the word into two halves, apply or8way to each, or their results and invert to get iszero — compact and easy to test.. In practical terms, combining or8way and not to test whether a word is zero. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Zero detect circuit
keyIdea.text: Split the word into two halves, apply Or8Way to each, Or their results and invert to get IsZero — compact and easy to test.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Zero Detection
Zero detection architecture
Split the 16‑bit input into high[8] and low[8]. Compute two Or8Way outputs, Or them, then invert to produce IsZero.
// Logical expression:
// IsZero = Not(Or(Or8Way(high[8]), Or8Way(low[8])))

// HDL idea: instantiate two Or8Way parts and a final Or and Not.
Example

For input 0x0000 both Or8Way outputs are 0, so IsZero becomes 1. For input 0x0001 a low half Or8Way yields 1, IsZero becomes 0.

Pitfall

Do not attempt to replace the final Not with inverted Or8Way outputs; be explicit to avoid inversion logic mistakes.

screens.title: Testing Multi‑bit Gates with the Hardware Simulator
screens.subtitle: Representative vectors, edge cases, and test script strategy

narration.text: Testing is essential. You will use the Hardware Simulator to load your HDL file and a matching test script that specifies inputs and expected outputs. For multi‑bit gates exhaustive testing is infeasible, so we rely on representative vectors and edge cases. The chapter suggests test patterns such as all zeros, all ones, alternating patterns like 0xAAAA and 0x5555, and single‑bit cases. These samples catch wiring errors, bit ordering mistakes, and wrong index ranges. A practical test strategy: first verify each 1‑bit gate exhaustively; then run these representative 16‑bit patterns on your multi‑bit implementation. Also add a few custom edge cases relevant to your wiring choices. For Or8Way and zero detection, include tests where only one input of the eight is high in different positions. A common misconception is to trust a single test pattern; rigorous testing uses multiple vectors that exercise different structural paths. When a simulator test fails, inspect the specific failing bit positions to localize which replicated instance has incorrect wiring. The reward for careful testing is confidence that your chip will behave when used in larger compositions like the ALU.

keyIdea.title: Testing method
keyIdea.text: Use exhaustive 1‑bit tests then representative multi‑bit vectors and targeted edge cases; inspect failing bit positions to isolate wiring errors.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Testing
Representative test vectors
  • 0x0000 — all zeros
  • 0xFFFF — all ones
  • 0xAAAA / 0x5555 — alternating patterns
  • Single bit high — check each output position
Debug workflow
  1. Test 1‑bit gates exhaustively.
  2. Run representative multi‑bit vectors.
  3. When a test fails, inspect which output bits differ to localize the faulty instance.
  4. Add targeted single‑bit tests to confirm fixes.

screens.title: Gate Count and Parallelism: Why And16 uses 32 Nand Gates
screens.subtitle: Relating 1‑bit implementations to multi‑bit area cost

narration.text: This lesson explains the gate‑count reasoning given in the chapter. A single 1‑bit And implemented from Nand requires two Nand gates: one Nand(a,b) to compute a temporary, then Nand(tmp,tmp) to invert that temporary and produce the And result. Because And16 is sixteen independent And gates operating in parallel, its internal Nand count is sixteen times two, which equals thirty‑two. This exact multiplication is important: And16 uses the same number of Nand gates as sixteen independent And gates because it literally instantiates sixteen copies. The practical insight is that parallel hardware increases throughput without changing logical depth, but area increases linearly. A common misbelief is that hardware implements optimizations to reuse gates across bits; without extra time multiplexing or sharing circuitry, bits remain independent. The consequence for architecture is clear: you pay area to gain single‑cycle word operations. As a short example: if you needed to reduce Nand count, you could time‑multiplex a single And over multiple cycles, but that changes the programming model and latency. Ask yourself: what tradeoffs will you accept when designing for speed versus area? Gate Count and Parallelism: Why And16 uses 32 Nand Gates means and16's nand count equals 16× the 1‑bit count because each bit is processed independently, illustrating the area-for-speed tradeoff.. In practical terms, relating 1‑bit implementations to multi‑bit area cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Area vs parallelism
keyIdea.text: And16's Nand count equals 16× the 1‑bit count because each bit is processed independently, illustrating the area-for-speed tradeoff.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Gate counting
Counting example
One 1‑bit And uses two Nand gates. Therefore And16 uses 16 × 2 = 32 Nand gates. This follows directly from replication: each bit gets its own hardware.
Contrast

Time‑multiplexing a single And reduces area but increases latency because you must sequence bit operations across cycles.

Takeaway

Parallel replication gives word‑wide single‑cycle behavior at the predictable cost of linear gate count increase.

screens.title: Hands‑on: Build and Test the Chips Listed
screens.subtitle: Stepwise lab plan to implement Not16, And16, Or16, Xor16 and Or8Way

narration.text: This lesson gives a concrete lab sequence you can follow. First, implement and exhaustively test each 1‑bit gate in HDL: Not, And, Or, and Xor. Second, write Not16 by instantiating Not sixteen times and verify with 0x0000 and 0xFFFF. Third, implement And16, Or16, and Xor16 by repeating the corresponding 1‑bit PARTS lines for indices 0 through 15; test with representative vectors such as 0xAAAA and 0x5555 plus single‑bit high values. Fourth, implement Or8Way as the balanced tree described in the chapter and test single‑input-high cases. Fifth, compose the zero detection circuit using two Or8Way blocks, one Or and a final Not and verify with the zero and nonzero patterns. Sixth, create custom tests for edge cases you suspect in your wiring. A typical pitfall is misindexing during replication; add tests that set single high bits at both LSB and MSB to expose such errors. Finally, reflect and document: draw the internal structure and record how many Nand gates each multi‑bit chip contains. This structured practice will build confidence and prepare you for the ALU construction that follows in later modules.

keyIdea.title: Lab plan
keyIdea.text: Follow a stepwise approach: 1‑bit tests, replicate to 16 bits, implement Or8Way, compose zero detect, and verify with representative and edge-case vectors.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.4 › Lab Plan
Stepwise tasks
  1. Implement and test 1‑bit gates exhaustively.
  2. Implement Not16 and test with 0x0000/0xFFFF.
  3. Implement And16/Or16/Xor16 and run representative vectors.
  4. Implement Or8Way and test single‑input highs.
  5. Compose zero detection with two Or8Way + Or + Not and verify.
  6. Document gate counts and draw internal structure.
Practical hints
  • Test single bits at both low and high indices to catch indexing errors.
  • Use the simulator log to see which outputs differ and localize failures.
  • Record expected gate counts as a cross‑check on your PARTS list.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, every basic gate — Not, And, Or, Xor — can be expressed using the Nand primitive, and those identities are the foundation for HDL implementations. Second, multi‑bit gates such as Not16, And16, Or16, and Xor16 are implemented by replicating the corresponding 1‑bit gate across the bus, producing parallel, single‑cycle behavior at linear area cost. Third, Or8Way is built as a balanced tree of two‑input Or gates and is the core building block for efficient zero detection when combined across halves.
